content: Dornase alfa is a mucolytic agent currently used to manage pulmonary disease in individuals with cystic fibrosis, which is the primary cause of morbidity and mortality in this population. Its mechanism of action involves reducing the viscosity of mucus in the lungs, thereby facilitating the clearance of airway secretions. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether dornase alfa improves mortality and morbidity in cystic fibrosis patients compared to placebo or other airway clearance therapies, and to identify any associated adverse events. A comprehensive search was conducted, including the Cochrane Cystic Fibrosis and Genetic Disorders Group Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. The most recent searches were performed on October 12, 2020, and February 8, 2021, respectively. Randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing dornase alfa to placebo, standard therapy, or other airway clearance medications were included. A total of 74 trials were identified, of which 19 trials involving 2565 participants met the inclusion criteria. Among these, 15 trials compared dornase alfa to placebo or no treatment (2447 participants), two trials compared daily dornase alfa to hypertonic saline (32 participants), one trial compared daily dornase alfa to both hypertonic saline and alternate-day dornase alfa (48 participants), and one trial compared dornase alfa to mannitol and the combination of both drugs (38 participants). The duration of these trials ranged from six days to three years. Dornase alfa versus placebo or no treatment: Dornase alfa likely improved forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) at one month (four trials, 248 participants), three months (one trial, 320 participants; moderate-quality evidence), six months (one trial, 647 participants; high-quality evidence), and two years (one trial, 410 participants). Limited low-quality evidence suggested that dornase alfa may have little or no impact on quality of life. Dornase alfa likely reduced the number of pulmonary exacerbations in trials lasting up to two years (moderate-quality evidence). One trial assessing the cost of care found that dornase alfa offset 18% to 38% of its medication costs. Daily versus alternate-day dornase alfa: A single cross-over trial involving 43 children found little or no difference between daily and alternate-day regimens in terms of lung function, quality of life, or pulmonary exacerbations (low-quality evidence). Dornase alfa versus other airway clearance medications: Results were mixed. One trial (43 children) suggested that dornase alfa might lead to greater improvement in FEV1 compared to hypertonic saline (low-quality evidence). Another trial (23 participants) reported little or no difference in lung function between dornase alfa and mannitol or dornase alfa combined with mannitol (low-quality evidence). One trial (23 participants) indicated that dornase alfa might improve quality of life compared to dornase alfa combined with mannitol (low-quality evidence), while other comparisons showed little or no difference in quality of life (low-quality evidence). No trials reported significant differences in the number of pulmonary exacerbations between dornase alfa and other treatments (low-quality evidence). Adverse events: Dornase alfa did not result in significantly more adverse effects compared to other treatments, except for an increased frequency of voice alteration and rash. Conclusions: Evidence suggests that dornase alfa improves lung function in cystic fibrosis patients compared to placebo in trials lasting from one month to two years. Pulmonary exacerbations were reduced in trials lasting six months or longer, likely due to the treatment. Voice alteration and rash were the only adverse events reported with increased frequency. There is insufficient evidence to definitively conclude whether dornase alfa is superior to other hyperosmolar agents in improving lung function.
